title: Adolescent Growth and Puberty
subject: Paediatrics
summary: Adolescent growth is a rapid phase of height, weight and bone development driven by hormonal changes. Recognising normal versus abnormal patterns guides early detection of endocrine, nutritional and skeletal disorders, especially in low‑resource settings.

sections.p: The adolescent growth spurt is a period of accelerated linear growth lasting 2–3 years, occurring earlier in girls (10‑12 y) than boys (12‑14 y). Diagnosis is clinical, using serial height measurements plotted on a growth chart.
b: Height velocity > 6 cm/yr in girls, > 7 cm/yr in boys indicates the peak growth period.
Bone age (Greulich‑Pyle) within 1 year of chronological age confirms normal timing.

sections.p: Growth disorders are staged by deviation from expected height velocity and final adult height.
b: Mild: velocity 5‑6 cm/yr (girls) or 6‑7 cm/yr (boys).
Moderate: velocity 3‑5 cm/yr or > 2 SD below target height.
Severe: velocity < 3 cm/yr or > 2 SD below target height with delayed bone age.

sections.p: Most adolescents have physiologic growth; pathology should be considered when velocity falls outside expected ranges.
b: Endocrine: hypothyroidism, growth hormone deficiency, hyperthyroidism.
Nutritional: chronic malnutrition, iron‑deficiency anemia (≈ 2 % of girls).
Chronic disease: HIV, TB, sickle cell disease, rheumatic heart disease.
Medications: long‑term glucocorticoids, antiepileptics.
Genetic: Turner syndrome, constitutional delay of growth and puberty.

sections.p: Patients may present with slowed height gain, short stature relative to peers, or delayed secondary sexual characteristics.
b: History of reduced growth velocity on school health records.
Physical: height < 3rd percentile, delayed bone age, low BMI.
Associated symptoms: fatigue, cold intolerance (hypothyroidism), menstrual irregularities (iron loss).

t.b: Is growth velocity adequate? – Decline > 1 cm/yr suggests pathology.
Is skeletal maturation appropriate? – Bone age > 2 years behind chronological age supports delayed growth.
Is hypothyroidism present? – Elevated TSH with low free T4 confirms.
Is growth hormone deficiency likely? – Low IGF‑1 with low GH peaks on stimulation test.
Is iron‑deficiency anemia contributing? – Hb < 12 g/dL (girls) or < 13 g/dL (boys) with low ferritin.
Is chronic infection affecting growth? – Positive test warrants ART and nutritional support.

t.a: If X‑ray unavailable, use mid‑upper arm circumference (MUAC)
t.b: Is severe malnutrition present? – MUAC < 12.5 cm in adolescents suggests.

sections.p: Unrecognised growth failure can lead to permanent short stature, psychosocial distress, and worsening of underlying disease.
b: Severe short stature (< -3 SD) with delayed bone age.
Signs of systemic disease (persistent fever, weight loss).
Rapidly progressive skeletal pain – consider osteosarcoma.

sections.p: Treat the underlying cause, optimise nutrition, and monitor growth.
b: Endocrine: levothyroxine for hypothyroidism; GH therapy for proven deficiency (only where available).
Nutritional: iron supplementation (ferrous sulfate) for iron‑deficiency; balanced diet with protein and calories.
Infection: ART for HIV, anti‑TB therapy, malaria prophylaxis where endemic.
Avoid long‑term steroids; if required, give calcium/vitamin D.
Counselling on sleep, physical activity and psychosocial support.

sections.p: Regular growth monitoring every 3–6 months until final height is reached.
b: Re‑measure height and weight, update growth chart.
Repeat bone age if growth remains < 5 cm/yr after 6 months.
Screen for anemia annually in menstruating girls.
Constitutional delay of growth and puberty – normal bone age, later onset of puberty.
Familial short stature – normal growth velocity, target height matches parents.
Skeletal dysplasias – abnormal limb proportions, radiographic metaphyseal changes.
Bone age may appear normal in early hypothyroidism; rely on clinical signs.
Ferritin can be elevated in infection, masking iron deficiency – use transferrin saturation.
IGF‑1 low in malnutrition; repeat after nutritional repletion before diagnosing GH deficiency.

whenToSeekHelp: Severe short stature with height < -3 SD and delayed bone age.
Rapidly worsening pain over long bones – risk of osteosarcoma.
Signs of systemic illness: persistent fever, weight loss, night sweats.

faq.q: Why does the growth spurt occur earlier in girls?
faq.a: Estrogen triggers epiphyseal plate closure earlier, so girls reach peak height velocity 1–2 years before boys.

faq.q: Can iron‑deficiency anemia really affect height?
faq.a: Yes, chronic anemia reduces oxygen delivery to growth plates, contributing to reduced velocity, especially in menstruating girls.

faq.q: What if I cannot obtain a bone‑age X‑ray?
faq.a: Use serial height velocity and clinical assessment; if growth remains < 5 cm/yr after 6 months, refer for specialist evaluation.

exam: A 13‑year‑old girl presents with height falling from the 50th to the 5th percentile over 6 months – what investigations would you order and why? — Assess growth velocity, obtain bone age, thyroid function, CBC with ferritin, and HIV test to identify endocrine, nutritional or infectious causes.

How does hypothyroidism alter adolescent growth, and what clinical clues help you differentiate it from constitutional delay? — Hypothyroidism causes slowed velocity, cold intolerance, dry skin; bone age lags > 2 years, whereas constitutional delay shows normal thyroid labs and later puberty.

A boy with sickle cell disease has stopped growing at 14 years; what management steps are essential? — Optimize hydroxyurea, ensure adequate nutrition, screen for iron deficiency, and consider endocrine referral for GH assessment.

Explain why iron‑deficiency anemia is common during the adolescent growth spurt in girls and how you would treat it in a low‑resource clinic. — Rapid growth increases iron demand; menstrual loss adds to deficit. Treat with oral ferrous sulfate, dietary counseling, and de‑worming if helminths are present.

What red‑flag symptom in an adolescent with rapid height gain should prompt evaluation for osteosarcoma? — New, localized bone pain or swelling, especially around the knee, warrants X‑ray and referral.

When is growth hormone therapy indicated in adolescents, and why might it be unavailable in low‑resource settings? — Indicated for confirmed GH deficiency with low IGF‑1 after stimulation testing; cost and need for monitoring limit use in many settings.

A patient on long‑term steroids presents with slowed growth – how would you modify therapy? — Reduce steroid dose if possible, add calcium/vitamin D, and consider alternative agents; monitor bone age and height.

Distinguish between familial short stature and growth failure due to chronic disease on a growth chart. — Familial short stature follows a normal growth curve parallel to target height; chronic disease shows a drop in velocity and falling percentiles.
